utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Ms. Edgerton, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask before we start with the cross-examination for permission to address the Trial Chamber briefly, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Poparic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, I would like to raise an issue related to the testimony yesterday that has to do with me personally. And I'm not sure that the Defence is going to raise that issue during the re-examination so I would like to raise it briefly now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what it's all about. Yesterday, Ms. Edgerton, when speaking about incident F6 claimed that I misstated something in my report, namely that Mrs. Sanija Dzevlan was going to visit her mother. She quoted from the transcript. She quoted her statement when she said that she was going to the hospital to get medicine. I checked the transcript yesterday, and it is correct that in one part of the transcript Ms. Sanija Dzevlan did say she was going to get medicine. However, in another part of the transcript, she confirmed to the Prosecutor, Mr. Mundis, that she was returning from the hospital after having visited her mother. I quoted that in my report. As a matter of fact, I did it so specifically that I even referred to the line of the transcript where this is mentioned. I don't know why Ms. Edgerton did not check that, and why she accused me of basically trying to deceive someone, which had never been my intention. You see, in this report that I quoted whatever I could quote. If I forgot something, that's a different matter, but I never had any intention of deceiving anyone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. But -- thank you, Mr. Poparic, but Ms. Edgerton never accused of you trying to deceive somebody else. Please don't misunderstand that. Yes, Ms. Edgerton, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Poparic.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to the sketch we left off looking at yesterday. That's P2421, page 3, and we were discussing incident F11. Because I want to give you just a little bit more of a chance to study this sketch because I actually think we might have misunderstood one another a little bit yesterday. Mr. Poparic, do you understand enough English so that my colleague can just enlarge the sketch that's on the screen in front of you? Or can you -- not -- the diagram isn't in English.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I apologise. But do you understand the diagram? Would that help you because I think maybe that might have been a result of -- might have been part of our misunderstanding yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So this diagram measures 1450 mils from the vertical line. You can see that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then yesterday, I told you that 1450 mils in a system of 6.000 was the same as an 87-degree angle of entry, but I realised only later that this report, having been prepared by French UNPROFOR officers, should have used the 6.400 mils system because the 6.000 system is the Serbian mils system, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And 1.450 mils converted into degrees using the 6400 mils system is between 81 and 82 degrees, which is 9 degrees horizontal. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. So that represents a very small angle, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We cannot look at it that way, small angle or not. I'll show you. We have the firing tables attached here for practically all the projectiles that were used. Since these were bursts of gunfire let us assume that this was an M84 machine-gun, and let us look at the angle of descent. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That doesn't really address my question but I think you want to refer to the tables so --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Here is the table, page 193 in my version, attachment 1. It says ballistic information for M84, 7.62 millimetres machine-gun, and we have the angles of descent. You see, all the way up to 700 metres, the angle is less than 1 degree. This angle that we see here is the sum total of less than 1 per cent and another angle, which is dictated by the position from which one fires and from the site point. If VRS positions were at 450 metres, if they were 450 metres away, if we look that the red building and then 30 to 40 metres, this particular angle could not be more than 3 or 4 degrees. So had the fire come from the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska, this angle would have to be less than 4 or 5 degrees. I don't know exactly now. So two times less than what had been established here. That is the only way which we can look at it and assess it, not just say whether it's a big or a small angle.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment. I just want to check something you said yesterday. So your answer to me now, again, is based on an assumption?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the assumption of a sight angle which is very objective, perhaps I gave one that is even greater so it can only be less than what I assumed. It's no problem to establish that accurately, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So whether or not - putting aside your response right now - this low angle, whether it's 4 or whether it's 9 degrees, is completely inconsistent with the shots having come from the Executive Council building, isn't it, according to your own analysis?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said yesterday that from the Executive Council building, one could fire from the ground floor and from upstairs, so it could be a 2-degree angle or an 80-degree angle, I mean the angle of descent. It depends on the height from which one fired because it's very close, this Executive Council building, and because of the close proximity, the angle is very big.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you didn't talk about a low-angle of descent from the Executive Council building in your analysis in your report.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have information about hits on the tram. Do you understand that? We did not know what the nature was of the hits on the first tram, 206, and the second one, 238, I think. We just had that video clip where you can see the impact on the ground, and we estimated the height on that basis. No one rules out the possibility that the tram was hit from different places. Even from this report, I don't know whether this is the first tram, 206, or the other one. On this other tram, I saw actually this document in General Mladic's trial, that the police on a technical sketch of the tram, they marked a lot of shots, hits, we don't know anything about them, so we could not claim that it was high up. As for the other tram, one could say, on the basis of the wounds of the casualty that it was from a great height. We don't know anything in this case, whether it's the first or second tram. But at any rate, this angle does not correspond to the angle that a projectile fired from the other bank of the Miljacka could have had.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Poparic, it seems like you're changing your evidence to suit the point --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- that you want to make.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't change anything. That's not true. I said that yesterday and I repeat it today.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this video from which you take two still images, and those are image 96 at page 138 of your report -- actually, and you could look at image 96 at page 138, it actually has a long discussion in French involving General Rose, General Gobillard and FrenchBat soldiers at the intersection of Djure Danicica Street. Do you understand French?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I understand some French but in the film that I had, I didn't have a sound-track so I had nothing to understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So then, without a sound track, you would have heard no mention of the Executive Council building in the film?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear it, but I just saw it showing in the direction of the Executive Council building. This officer is actually showing General Rose, I mean he's pointing at the building. We can see this in the picture. It may resemble an opening or something like that. Actually, he was pointing in the direction of Grbavica or, rather, that red building they mentioned was divided between the VRS and the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, so what you -- your conclusion is actually an assumption based on what you saw, nothing more? That's what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot confirm at all what he said to him. I can just say that he was pointing in that direction and I know that after that, General Rose sent a letter of protest to both sides in relation to the firing at the tram, nothing else. This is just an illustration of what was happening in that area during the investigation or, rather, the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you just repeat the words you said after, "... during the investigation...," if there indeed was anything?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just an illustration of what was happening in that area during the investigation and after the investigation, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. Then talking about after the investigation, having reviewed the materials related to this incident, you would have seen that on October 10th, General Rose met with General Mladic in Jahorina and he began the meeting by condemning the incident on the tramway that we have been talking about, which caused one death and seven injuries. Doesn't -- didn't seeing that kind of evidence cause you to rethink your assumption which was based on dust clouds?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of evidence you mean. If you mean this film --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let me just show you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we call up P867, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Poparic, my time today is extremely limited, so please accept that if you feel I may have interrupted you, I'm just trying to keep focused. P867, there is a B/C/S translation, but this is an UNPROFOR report on a meeting General Rose had with General Mladic on 10 October 1994. And if you go over to page 2 in English and page 3 in B/C/S, paragraph 5, you see that, as I said, General Rose began his remarks by condemning the sniping incident we've been discussing; General Mladic denied that the Serbs were involved; he claimed that the shooting had come from the Holiday Inn; and in the very last paragraph you see an UNPROFOR technical expert was present -- pardon me, was -- an UNPROFOR technical expert present was able to assure the party that the shooting did not come from the Holiday Inn side, a map was provided. Doesn't that cause you to rethink your assumption, Mr. Poparic?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not aware of this document but I see from here that the only thing that was proven was that there was no firing from the Holiday Inn which is correct, and that corresponds to our findings, but there is no evidence that would indicate that it was certainly fired from the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. We'll move on. I'd like to talk to you about another incident. It's scheduled incident F1 which took place on 13 December 1992. It's the first incident you deal with in your report, and it deals with the location of Baba Stijena. And as I understand the thrust of your argument with respect to this incident is there was no line of sight because it was either blocked from dense tree cover or a terrain elevation; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The core of the matter is that the configuration of the terrain is such that this house cannot be seen from Stijena Baba and that was confirmed in three different ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Poparic, what I'd like to do is show you an image, 65 ter number 25134. Now, Mr. Poparic, did you actually personally visit the incident site in this case, the location at which the girl was at the moment she was shot?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So having done that, you would have seen that --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- the house has been renovated since the time of the incidents and it's no longer possible to stand or crouch at that specific location?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you just repeat just the comment you made that spoke over me just now? Just repeat what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Wait just a second. Please wait.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Poparic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is correct that the house looks different now and that there was some renovation done.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Poparic, here are three images, one on top of the other, all showing a line of sight from the specific incident location, with the exception of your photograph down below. Could you go back up to the top one, please, to Baba Stijena. The first one which is 65 ter 10059 was used with the father, Ekrem Pita, during -- at the time he gave a statement to the OTP, and Mr. Pita marked, as you can see, Baba Stijena from his porch. The second one -- pardon me, and this first photograph was taken in 2001, September 2001. The second one - if you can go down, Madam Registrar [sic] - is the photograph taken in November 2006 by Mr. van der Weijden when he visited the scene, so both these photographs were taken before the renovations to the territory. And that comes from P1620, page 15. And if we could go down to the bottom of the page, the last one is your photograph --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- taken from page 57 of your report. Now, but for the fact that the vegetation has grown over the intervening years between 2001 and whenever you took this photograph, so I assume either 2010 or 2011, they all show a line of sight to Baba Stijena. So your maps are completely inconsistent with this photographic record, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have put quite a few questions, haven't you, so I have to start from the beginning. The photograph marked by Ekrem Pita, first of all, in that photograph, if you can show it up here, what we can see is that Mr. Ekrem Pita marked a completely different direction for Baba Stijena, somewhere up in the sky, you see? This house on the left-hand side it is totally in this direction but he marked it in the opposite direction. That shows that he did not know exactly where Stijena Baba is because this Stijena Baba cannot actually be seen. What Mr. Ekrem Pita marked is completely different from what I filmed and from what Mr. Weijden filmed. The photographs that were taken by Mr. Weijden and myself are completely identical. The only difference -- the basic difference is that Mr. Weijden took this picture with a 6-times zoom and I used a normal zoom. And that's the only difference that can be observed as regards these two photographs. The photograph that was taken with the zoom shows all these objects that are closer to each other and you can see that, if you look at the two photographs. In my photograph it can be seen behind -- actually what can be seen behind that is a small clearing and then a forest, a small forest. There is another difference. Mr. Weijden took the picture when there was no vegetation; whereas mine is greener, there is some vegetation. However, in terms of position it's one and the same thing. So Stijena Baba does not have a real clearing, you can see that on the basis of some of the photographs here. What Mr. Weijden showed as Stijena Baba is not Stijena Baba. In one photograph --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, you're repeating your report. Let's go back to these photographs. Are you disagreeing with me that these photographs show the same location?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photographs are -- were taken from the same location but they do not both show Stijena Baba. The one at the top is where Ekrem Pita marked it somewhere to the right and high up and you can see where Stijena Baba is as marked by Mr. van der Weijden. It is between the buildings and on the photograph at the top we can only see the building and nothing else, the house. So it is to the far right as compared to what Mr. van der Weijden had taken. As for Mr. van der Weijden's photograph, I agree that it is the direction of Stijena Baba, and I photographed it as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your disagreement is on the basis of the marking that Mr. Pita put on the photograph and nothing else?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also because one can't see anything. If Mr. Pita had known exactly where Stijena Baba was, he would not have made such a big mistake. It's an enormous mistake, in terms of direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. So your position is that these photographs don't show Baba Stijena?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your position is that a resident of the area mismarked Baba Stijena?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll move on, but to be able to understand the witness's evidence could this be a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6367, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd now like to go on to incident F9 which is discussed in your report at paragraphs 1236 -- pardon me, 126 to 133, and it relates to an incident on 26 June 1994 where the origin of fire is alleged to have been from the school for the blind in Nedzarici. And while you acknowledged in your evidence and in your report that there is a line of sight from the specific location of the incident to the school for the blind, that's transcript page 38980, and that the distance is relatively short, which you said on the same page. You also said it didn't seem logical to you that there would have been a sniper position there and that you hadn't seen any document, photograph or film that would indicate it was used as such. And that's all on the same transcript page, 38980, also at paragraph 131 of your report. Now, I take it from this you don't exclude the possibility that there was a sniper operating from that location; you've just never seen the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see the evidence and it does not strike me logical from the point of view of tactical use. I cannot exclude the possibility of course that someone did fire from there. No one could exclude that without evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine. Could we have a look quickly at P1601? It's an UNMO HQ, BH command daily sit-rep dated 13 July 1994, so two weeks after this incident. At page 4 of this document in both languages, paragraph 24, thank you, and in B/C/S it's at the very bottom of paragraph 24(b), you see a report that the commander of the 1st battalion of the BSA, Ilidza brigade admitted the sniping by the BSA. Could we go over to the next page in B/C/S, please? From grid reference BP 859578, house for blind people, he promised that there would be no more sniping from that place. So it seems once again that your opinion is -- pardon me, is your opinion now informed by the evidence you've seen as to whether there was a sniper operating from that specific location?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask for one clarification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am wondering if the Prosecution made use of the possibility of having that brigade commander here to check or double check whether it's true what he admitted to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. This is not an appropriate intervention, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Mr. Poparic, can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. In the document, it seems that he acknowledged they opened fire from the house for the blind. However, it is not specified in what direction, because the building for the blind offers a different view, which is more important for their side. It is a forward post offering that kind of vantage point. It -- we did not have any specific direction provided or the time when there was fire opened. Obviously according to the report, fire was opened but we cannot say with any certainty that fire was opened on the 26th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, just in regard to your comment about direction, I'd like to show you something. It's 65 ter 25090. And I take it you base your comment about direction -- we'll wait till the image comes up. Mr. Poparic, this is a video taken from -- it's a still taken from a video of the school for the blind taken just after the reintegration in 1996, and it's part of 65 ter 40599, and it's a -- it was a documentary on students moving back into the school. Now, if we can enlarge, please, the right-hand side of this image a little bit further and you would agree with me, wouldn't you, Mr. Poparic, that that right-hand side of the building where you see a wall as opposed to the windowed side, a wall, that's the side most exposed to the incident site of F9; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This side is exposed. However, if you look at the window up at the top on the left it was cleared away, confirming that something may have been there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please repeat the rest of his answer? We did not catch it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The interpreters have asked to you repeat the rest of your answer because they didn't catch it, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The upper left-hand corner of the photograph, we see a destroyed window which confirms my assumption that that position would not have been a favourable one to mount a sniping position because it is easy to destroy it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you said in your answer to me a couple of minutes ago, that the school for the blind offers a different view, and in regard to the direction, I just want you to look at these holes in the side of the wall most exposed to the incident site. You can see openings made by bricks being knocked out. That's evidence of firing positions, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have in mind this opening here, on the first window --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, I'm asking you to look at the wall of the building that's most exposed to the incident site?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The side one, on the side?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the side wall, there seem to be some openings, perhaps something was knocked out, I really can't say. As for the bottom openings, down, they were definitely not visible from the position where it is claimed that the girls were at when fired at. Perhaps there was another opening further up but I'm not sure whether the height allows a view of the location where they were hit, and I don't know whether something was knocked out or whether the hole was created by a projectile. The photograph is very poor. This side faces another direction, that is to say Alipasino Polje. If even if there openings on that side, I don't see how someone could take up a position in order to see the girls moving in another direction, because they were at an angle of almost 90 degrees in relation to the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I just have a moment, Your Honours, because my LiveNote has stopped. I was on my own LiveNote and I just need to look at Mr. Reid's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Same with mine. We will restart it and let us see whether it works. Can we continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely. I just wanted to make sure that everything was all right technically speaking on the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Poparic, you actually didn't answer my question about firing positions so maybe I can ask it a different way. These holes that you see on the side of the building are consistent with evidence of firing positions, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that it was possible. We can't see anything. Now that we are discussing firing positions I can tell you that from the place where it is claimed as the place where the girls were hit, we can only see the upper part of the wall, up to the top of the window. Second of all, on the window we see no protection, no sacks. I don't see how someone could fire from there through an exposed window.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. But Mr. Poparic, in paragraph 7 of your report, it's on page 30 of the English but paragraph 7, you made exactly the same argument I'm putting to you in respect of this image, and it's exactly the same position you took with respect to the holes in the image -- pardon me, in the photo of the faculty building that's at image 67.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Go over to -- if I could suggest, Mr. Poparic -- your report -- Mr. Poparic --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, could you go over to page 36 of your report in your language, image 6. So I'll give you the references in your language as opposed to the English ones.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Photograph number 6 and?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. That's --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And 67?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You made exactly the same argument with respect to firing positions that I'm putting to you now.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, I do not deny that. I'm only saying that on the photograph I can't see the openings; however, on the other one I can see it. The first photograph is of poor quality so I can't make it out. I can't say if it was created by a detonating projectile or whether the bricks were knocked out. I really can't see it. That is the only difference. I do not claim that the bricks could not have been knocked out and now that we are discussing directions in principle, it was possible and that's how things were done, but based on the photograph you showed me I cannot state decisively that it was knocked out. There are some traces there, some hits, but I really can't see whether the bricks were knocked out or whether it's a different kind of damage. I can't even see whether it's a through hole or if it's just surface damage.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, you can't see whether it's a through hole on the image, your image 6, either, Mr. Poparic. You're looking for the differences to take a position that helps Dr. Karadzic, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On photograph number 6, we can see that the hole is large and with regular edges, which indicates that something was knocked out. If you show us your photograph, you can see that we can barely see the traces. That's the difference. So the issue on hand is the quality of photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we go back to the photograph of the school for the blind, please? 25090. Thank you. Could I have this marked as a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I'll be ten more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could we have the exhibit number again?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6368, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With Your Honour's permission, I think I will take ten more minutes to conclude, if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I want to go on to scheduled incident F14. That's a tram sniping incident on 23 November 1994. And you deal with it in your report from paragraph 175. Now, the -- I just want to ask you about Mrs. Karacic. One of your claims is that she - she is one of the two women in the tram - was facing to the rear of the tram, so facing east, and she was hit by a bullet that entered her right shoulder and exited through her upper right arm, and you say that at paragraph 181 of your report. Now, you never -- you've said that you never met any of the survivors of these incidents, so obviously you've never seen the entry and exit wounds of Mrs. Karacic; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I based it on the official report. It is not my finding, it is the official finding.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And there were no measurements in that report showing the vertical distance that the bullet fragment travelled inside her arm, are there?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, as far as I know. I have no other information.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your conclusion that the vertical distance the bullet travelled was more than 1.76 centimetres was based on her statement, and you quoted it in your report. You said, as you say, the bullet entered the upper part of her shoulder and exited from the lower part of her upper arm. That's paragraph 182. So your conclusion about the distance travelled is based on that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is based on that statement and on general knowledge of anatomy. We know where the upper part of an arm is and what the distance is. It is obvious.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. And so your -- additionally, your analysis also assumes that her arm was in a straight vertical downwards position by her side when the bullet fragment struck her; right? She wasn't holding on to any part of the tram, she wasn't scratching her ear, she wasn't adjusting her clothing, your assumption is that her arm was straight downwards by her side?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assumption was that her arm was in a normal position. It is not based only on her injury. There is the injury of another person similar in nature, and it is more likely that they were in that position. So she was not the only one with that kind of injury. The next person had it too.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, but you don't know that she couldn't have been doing any one of the things that I described, any number of things that people can do all the time with their arms when they are riding on public transport; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I think I explained that, that the bullet came from -- had the bullet come from the side where she said it had, it would not have ended up in the upper arm. It would have ended up somewhere in the body itself. Irrespective of what she was doing with the arm, had she been hit in the shoulder, the bullet would have ended up inside the body, because that was the angle of the tram as compared to the buildings suspected as having been the source of fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll move on to one final incident, that's sniping incident F15, which is the next one chronologically speaking and the next one in your report and it took place on 27 February 1995. And this is the incident where in your testimony, it's a tram sniping incident, and in your testimony you agreed that this was probably an automatic rifle or a machine-gun that strafed the tram, and that's at transcript page 39000, and that's also where you claimed at transcript page 38999 that one of the traces that the police marked as an exit point was actually something that was made with a felt-tip marker pen, and you also referred to that in regard to image 108 of your report. So --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Based on your evidence about the felt-tip marker pen, if you're right, this must have been an intentional manipulation of the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd rather not go into that. I am only discussing what I can see in the photograph. I see the number 3 and I see the comment in photo documentation. It is stated that it was marked with a number 3, indicating the place where the projectile went out at the same height as the height on the outer side of the tram. That's what we find in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, you did get into it because you said -- because you mentioned it. You said that the exit point is a dot that was marked with a felt-tipped marker pen. So -- but there is no way that a professional officer would accidentally make a mark on a wall and confuse it for a real hole; right? So you're alleging an intentional manipulation of the crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he would have done and how he arrived at this. It's a fact that this was marked with a marker and that the exit point is down there where we see it and that they wrote that what had been marked with a marker was the exit point, which it isn't. I don't know if it's a mistake or something else. I don't want to go into that. But these are the facts. There is a marking made with a marker, and the exit point is lower down, and they marked the -- marked it with a number 3 - I mean the marker trace - but the angle of descent was such that the bullet couldn't have come from the white high-rise buildings. The exit point is lower down and not what has been marked here, and that's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, you keep saying these are facts but that's just your evidence, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is other evidence too, and I said as much. In this case --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We measured the -- both lines, how thick they are, and the thickness -- their thickness matches. We stated that thickness and we haven't made that up. It's all measured.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the effect -- assuming you're correct, the effect of that marking would be to conceal the evidence that -- the evidence -- to conceal the evidence with regard to the angle of descent and to conceal the evidence that the shots came from a nearby Bosnian building. If you're right, that's the effect of that marking?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that the intention was to conceal anything. I'm saying that the point of entry and the point of exit are at approximately the same height -- what has also been mentioned and the photo documentation. And that position of these two points indicates that the shot was fired from the white high-rise buildings at Grbavica. They don't go into details. I don't know what their intention was. But to me, this is evidence that fire was not opened from the white high-rise buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You said fire was opened from the Museum of Revolution or some other building, and that's at paragraph 189 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in your testimony you added another possible building. You said -- I just want to look at a picture of the Museum of Revolution, and that appears as image 106 at page 155 of your report. Do you see it on the screen in front of you? So your claim --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your claim is that a Bosnian forces machine-gunner could sit on top of that building and strafe a passing tram without being detected by anyone on this main thoroughfare; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have been lying or been in a different position, not necessarily sitting. And I mentioned that building as one of the options. It's merely an assumption. And the opening of fire was very short. He opens fire, immediately hides, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just one more photograph and then we will be done. From P1738, which is also one of the items you sourced in your -- one of the exhibits you sourced in your report. The photo is on page 109 of P1738 that I want to look at. And the English version of -- the English translation of the text below the photo is at page 104. This, in one of the reports you sourced, is an image from a sniper's nest on the 10th floor of the building at Grbavica 8 where you see a view of a tram passing in front of the Museum of Revolution. So if there had been a machine-gunner lying or in a different position, not necessarily sitting on that building, the Museum of Revolution, in full view of SRK forces, he wouldn't have been there for very long, would he have?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a hypothesis now. I never claimed that he must have been right here. This photograph shows that he could have been here because you see there is like a fence on the roof or, rather, a low wall. He could have been there and fired a burst of fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm about -- he could have been targeted from this high-rise building but it's to be expected that he didn't stay there long, if he was there in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, could you tell us the reference number or the footnote number where Mr. Poparic referenced to this -- made reference to this photo?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I can. It will take me a couple of minutes because it's at a different part of his report, but I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I take it that you have re-examination, Mr. Karadzic, for this witness. But before we hear your re-examination, the Chamber is minded to take an early break, if it is -- if it poses another problem. We will take a break for half an hour and resume at 10.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just to answer your query from just before we left, Your Honour, P1738 was sourced in footnotes 32 and 34 of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Poparic.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please pause a bit longer before answering.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see image 108 from this document? I would like to start with the most recent things to continue with the other parts of the cross-examination. Image 108. The page number is 157 in Serbian, and in English it's part of paragraph 188. One is enough. And please enlarge it sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, did you have satisfactory documentation from the point of view of the nature of the injury or, to put it differently, do we know exactly in which part of the body Rabija Ilalagic [phoen] was wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Talking about this case, we didn't even have the photo documentation. We only had black and white photos where nothing could be seen. We got these photographs by mere chance with a witness who had nothing to do with this case. We obtained these better quality photographs by chance but what we had received originally was not usable at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us if we know the trajectory of the projectile inside the tram?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not inside the tram, but what's important for this case, the police stated that ten bullets were registered, of which seven hit the panelling, two probably went through the glass. Of these eight, four stayed in the panelling and the rest went through. The fact that four bullets didn't go through the panelling shows that the angle of descent was great, and that's why they stayed inside the panelling. If the bullet had been fired from the white high-rise buildings, it would have hit the tram at a very small angle of descent, and would have pierced the panelling at almost the same height as the point of entry. This photograph and the description in the official report shows that the bullet was fired from a small distance and at a great angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does mark 9 signify?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Probably the bullet went through the opening of the radiator, and judging by this photograph I would say that this is where it ended up, but I don't exactly remember everything from the photo documentation. It must be a trace of that bullet which fell on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is there a deformity in front of mark 9?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell. It's very dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please zoom in on the photograph? There must be a reason for this number 9.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, maybe this is because of the stamp but probably it's some trace of the bullet that went through the panelling. At any rate, this isn't important for an assessment of where the bullet came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But if it ended up here, then the first variant is even better for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The angle of descent would be even greater. But let's not forget that the outer bullet-hole is somewhat higher than the inner one. But the angle is great. If we compare the outer hole which is shown in image 107 and the trace on the radiator then we can tell that the angle was great.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can zoom out now and let me ask you if you can mark the trajectory from the exit point in the radiator to the outer panelling and on to this deformity in the seat support, with a dotted line. That is, draw a full line inside the tram and a dotted line for the trajectory --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- in the panelling.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We can suppose that this was the trajectory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm just looking in the transcript of a few minutes ago to see where I asked a single question in cross-examination for this incident and about the trajectory of the bullet, and the cross-examination was only about the marking, Your Honour, the felt-tip marker marking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it boils down to the issue of trajectory at the end of the day. But, yes, Mr. Robinson, could you help us?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I was just thinking the same thing. You can't limit re-examination that fine so that we can only contest those things that she has pointed to if the answer is found in another aspect of the same incident. So I think that you're correct that issue of the trajectory was raised by the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will allow the accused to continue. Yes, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just explain. I also drew this angle alpha. This is an approximate angle. If mark 9 or if number 9 marks a projectile trace, then obviously the angle is greater. That's why I drew it here and marked it alpha.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please date and initial this document.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today is the 6th or the 5th?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3647, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now get P6367? Three photographs. P6367. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please take a look at all these three photographs, start with your own, and continue with van der Weijden's and finish with Pita's. Can you mark from what direction you think the bullet came and from which direction it came according to Pita?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The interpreters just asked for the witness to repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just said to this lady that it was all right. I marked a rock in my photograph. It is number 1. And this rock can be also seen on Mr. van der Weijden's photograph. I can mark it 2. And the third photograph, this rock cannot be seen. But there is an arrow drawn by Mr. Pita indicating the direction in which the Baba rock is. I marked it 3. The directions match in my photograph and that of Mr. van der Weijden, whereas there is a significant difference in Mr. Pita's photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please can you indicate the direction as marked by Pita in your photograph and Mr. van der Weijden's?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area that Pita marked cannot be seen here, but I will mark -- I will draw arrows that approximately match our direction. I'll mark them with a number 4 and a number 5, respectively. Whereas what Mr. Pita marked would roughly correspond to this. I mark these with the numbers 6 and 7 respectively. There is an error of about 20 to 30 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please date and initial this.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not getting your --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if the portion outside the white area will be recorded or saved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be saved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I -- should I sign once more?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's okay. We will receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3648, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, 1D6926, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a view of the Sarajevo valley from Grdonj. Could we please zoom in on the left-most third? Can we scroll down a bit or maybe we can do it like this. Can you see in this photograph of Trebevic from Grdonj, can you see the Baba rock? Stijena Baba? Perhaps we can scroll down on the photograph some more. No, I want to go further down. Perhaps -- no, the other way around, I need the upper part. Some more, some more. The other -- lower down. Can you recognise the Lukavica-Pale road?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid this is too high up. Perhaps here, Stijena Baba, around here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have to use the pen. We cannot see. We do not see what you're doing.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to tell what it is. It is very, very small.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I kindly ask you to go from right to left?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that but I'm trying -- it's very hard for me to see. This seems to be the plateau where that motel was. And then it would be here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe this is Stijena Baba but it is barely visible. I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know where this is, Zagrici?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zagrici? Zagrici is down here, way down here, below this road, that's where it should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When it's barely visible, I'm wondering, whether there is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether there is a point to continue this exercise, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, if there is no certainty and visibility then I will give up, although it would be useful this photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance? There was a photograph that I took and that was displayed in the courtroom. Unfortunately it's not here right now, and it was also taken from Spicasta Stijena, Grdonj. Stijena Baba can be seen very nicely. At an altitude of 50 to 100 metres there is a smaller Stijena or rock, probably what Mr. Weijden and I took a picture of, I did not deal with that because I had other things indicating that that's not Stijena Baba but there is a similar Stijena rock in a similar direction and similar to Stijena Baba and that's probably the one that we took a picture of. There is a photograph, I don't know whether it can be used but it certainly does exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In whose territory was this smaller rock?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the territory of the BH Army because Stijena Baba was the separation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, actually we are going to give up on this. This can be removed. On page 87 of yesterday's transcript, part of a UN report about the incident of the 18th of November, 1994, was read out to you. Did you have any insight regarding the investigation material or, actually, did the UN investigate the incident?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I know that it was the Bosnian police working on this, but they also did not have access to the site, on the basis of the investigator who took part in the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: P004459, could we have a look at that, 00459. Prosecution report. Let us not call up this UN document. Do you remember that it was put to you that the French Battalion responded vis-a-vis the Serb positions, they fired back?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I said it was from a 14.5-millimetre machine-gun, and I said then that bursts of gunfire could be heard in that film that was shown. However, in the film, there is no gunfire coming from that 14.5-millimetre machine-gun and you cannot see that it was fired at that moment because 14.5 millimetre -- it's actually mounted on an APC or a tank and then it would have to be then and it's possible that they fired after that gunfire that was heard in that film so we cannot link this incident to that gunfire on the basis of what we have available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at page 4 now or actually the fifth page of this report or, rather, this document? I'm going to read it out to you. Could you please find that same page in English? It's probably the first page. Underneath these names in line 10, it says: "At the moment when they were crossing Franje Rackog Street or, rather, when they stopped stepped on the sidewalk on the other side of the street, a shot was -- a shot came from the direction of Grbavica." Is this something that you saw?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm familiar with these findings but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just to avoid any misunderstanding on the part of the witness, I think Dr. Karadzic should be clear that when they stepped to the pavement on the other side of the street, on the side closer to the earth museum, a shot was heard; because as Dr. Karadzic read it out that indicates not necessarily the side of the street that the document reports them as being on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a translation mistake. The APC of the Ukrainian Battalion was near the museum and it changes the entire meaning. The wounded were already on the other side of the street, and that is how these translations, these mistranslations, change the actual situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, I don't think that's a mistranslation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I find it difficult to follow. If there is a -- if you are saying that there is a mistranslation, why don't we ask the witness to read out the sentence. The paragraph -- the relevant part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Poparic, could you find this part where it says, "At the moment...," et cetera, and then read to these numbers, 225 or whatever it was. So, "At the moment...," read it slowly so that the interpreters can interpret it correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's find out whether we are on the correct page. English page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, towards the bottom of the page and in Serbian it's the entire paragraph. It is the lower part of the second paragraph. That was fine in English. Could you go back to the first page in English that we had on the screen, the lower part in English. [In English] "At the moment they were crossing ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, could you start reading, Mr. Poparic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "At the moment when they were crossing Franje Rackog Street, more precisely when they stepped on to the pavement on the other side of the street, from the direction of Grbavica or, rather, from the aggressor positions, a shot was heard. The mother and the boy were hit by the same round, fell to the ground, and the two men approached them to give them first aid. At the time the shot was heard from Franje Rackog Street, on the side that is closer to the national museum ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English can we have the next page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "... there was APC of the Ukrainian Battalion, registration number..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please go on to the end of this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Registration number UNPF 6495, while on the pavement of Franje Rackog Street, there was not a single UNPROFOR vehicle. Soon after the incident, two armoured personnel carriers of the UNPROFOR French Battalion, licence plate numbers UNPF 15225 and UNPF 15841, arrived on the screen and parked at Franje Rackog Street."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 1 in English back on our screens now? Could we enlarge the lower part? Your Excellencies, now I'm going to show you what was interjected, what is not in the original: [In English] "At the moment they were crossing Franje Rackog Street, more precisely when they stepped on the pavement on the other side of the street," and now we have implanted another that does not exist in original, "on the side closer to the earthly museum." [Interpretation] A completely invented sentence. If someone finds it in the original, I will admit to all the sins of this world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think when reading out it's connected to some later part. I'm not sure how much it changes the meaning, but we will take a look at this later on. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, this museum is mentioned, but only in relation to the position of the APC of the Ukrainian Battalion. However, this is just interjected. If you compare it to what the witness read out and also demand from the service to tell you what this is all about, and I wonder who did this and for what purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, do you remember that they said there that French UNPROFOR was there and that they responded with fire towards the Serbs and here this report says that they came after the incident?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could we please take a look at page 91? You were told, it was suggested to you that the French put these small sticks into bullet-holes to see what the direction was. Could we please have that photograph now, with that dust?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's photograph 95, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe so. What's the page?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 137 in our version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 137 in Serbian, and what's the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The paragraph is 154.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could this please be zoomed in, I mean the photograph? And I'm asking you kindly to activate the blue pen. Before that, a physics question, Mr. Poparic. The angle of descent and the angle of ascent, is there a correlation in terms of reflection?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is an analogy not only as far as light is concerned but also in such cases dust, and so on. For example, specifically, now that we are discussing projectiles, ricochet is an example of that. It behaves analogously to light, so the angle of descent of the projectile when it ricochets, it is approximately equal to the angle of ricochet except in some cases when it's an irregular impact, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we see this photograph enlarged over the entire screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's enlarge it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please activate the blue pen now and underneath this oval shape, this ellipse, could you draw a horizontal line that would be long enough from the green area to the other side of the tracks?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be it roughly. Should I mark it with a number 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Could you now draw a perpendicular line?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the right side of the ellipse so that we do not disturb the image in any way?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a bit on the pavement, too, but never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 3 now, towards the right, could you draw a line that would be under a, say, 10-degree angle?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If fire came from the other side of the Miljacka River it could not be more than a 5-degree angle. We saw according to the tables it's less than 1 degree and then there is also the sight angle, so it should be like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 3 then, could you place number 3 there and could you also mark it as less than 10 degrees?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to put that it's approximately 5, that would be the angle, and I can also put that it's less than 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you now determine this column, how close it is to 90 degrees?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very close. If we compare it to this trajectory number 2, it's almost parallel. However, number 3, how that would continue, had the projectile arrived along 3, since it's a small angle, it would go through the ground and practically it would ricochet this way. This would be direction number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you put your initials there and the date?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D3649, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did have you an insight into different expert reports that were produced by expert witnesses on the Prosecution side?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. Which ones do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any of them spend the war period in Sarajevo, any of those experts?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think only Berko Zecevic did, who resides in Sarajevo and he spent the war there, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the foreign expert witnesses did not spend the war there, or do you have any information that they did spend the war there or did they see -- that they saw anything?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have that information, which does not exclude the possibility that none of them were there at some point in time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Karadzic kindly repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll be happy to. You were asked by the Prosecution whether you were there during the war. Can you tell us what the source of your information was? What did you use?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source of my information was the material offered in this case, that is to say official reports, UNPROFOR reports, the transcript, witness statements and testimony, photographs, footage, et cetera, et cetera. Plus I visited the locations. So whatever I could get my hands on is what I used in the analysis. There was quite a lot of material.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In which -- which of the incidents involved full forensic documentation, and medical documentation, which could undoubtedly determine the angle, trajectory and type of injury?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And that's what confused me the most. In the plethora of material, I did not come across any forensic analysis. There were numerous findings cited from those reports but I did not see a single forensic medical report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the range resulting in an acceptable precision of an automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, depends which kind of automatic rifle. If we are talking about an automatic rifle M70 which is 70.62 millimetres in calibre and which was the most frequent weapon, it can be used to distances up to 800 metres. Objectively speaking, it can be used at distances up to 400 metres. That is its basic use. Next, we have weapons that are more powerful than the automatic rifle and the machine-gun, which is M-84, which can be used at ranges up to 1500 metres. But its useful range, efficient range, is 1.000 metres. In the firing tables, for that type of machine-gun, the possible dispersion is cited only up to the distance I mentioned because if one goes further, at longer distances, dispersion is greater and it is believed that it is not optimally used. It can be used in some very specific situations but no great precision is expected of that machine-gun at ranges over 1.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The firing tables are attached to the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm referring to the incident involving Ms. Dzevlan next. In the arsenal of the VRS or the JNA, was there a sniper rifle which could fire bursts of fire?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In principal there is no point for a sniper rifle to fire bursts of fire because it decreases precision which is the basic purpose of a sniping rifle. The JNA and VRS sniper rifle that we used the most was M76, which is a semi-automatic rifle with ten rounds in its cartridge, in its magazine. The fact that it is semi-automatic simply decreases the amount of time spent between two rounds fired. So it increases the possibility of firing the next round more quickly, after having corrected the firing elements as needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In e-court can we have D670? Can you confirm -- I'll read it out -- ah, yes we see it in English, too. Can you confirm that it is stated here that Sanija was returning home at around 4.30 p.m. The statement was provided, I think, in 19 --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 30th of September, 1994. The first line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Is it stated here that first she heard ricochetted bullets and then she was hit? I'll read it out.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you don't need to. It is correct. She was moving down Nikolje Demonja Street when bullets started to fly, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. She does not mention the church but she actually believed it was fire from Dobrinja 4. Can you tell us how far it was from that location?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dobrinja 4 that she referred to was some 480 metres away. It is a specific location because it is visible from Serb positions but only at an angle of 6 degrees. If we take into account what was visible from the incident location, it encompasses the angle of 6 degrees. What is interesting there? Because the separation line was on the street itself, on one side was the VRS, on the other the BiH army, as testified by General Ismet Hadzic. In that kind of situation, I don't think anyone opened fire. It would be unreasonable to open fire from either side at a distance of ten metres. They probably talked to each other rather than firing at each other. When it comes to this incident, we have no medical documentation, which would give us any indication as to the nature of wounds. If there was a trace on the left-hand side of the body, and if it is higher up than the trace on the right-hand side of the body, then the projectile came from this area. Even if we knew that, it would be impossible to determine who fired the round because the position of both sides was basically at the same place, ten metres apart. That's what Ms. Edgerton asked me, whether it was important to use the GPS to determine the position 2 metres this or that way. It is not. It only changes the descent point by a few centimetres. If we had forensic medical documentation then it would be possible to determine who fired the burst, otherwise we can't. Obviously in this case we had a burst of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, where on this document does the lady talk about the ricochetted bullet at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will read it out, "When bullets started falling around me, that were fired from Dobrinja...," and in some other statements she said that she he could hear "bullets bouncing off the tarmac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's on the other document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please be cautious not to be leading. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we next have a page from the Galic testimony - it is 92 ter in this case - page 3518 of the transcript. Perhaps I can read it out for you. Answer to the question as to when it happened: [In English] "I think it was between 3.00 and 4.00 in the afternoon."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That has an exhibit number in this case and I'm just trying to find it. Perhaps Dr. Karadzic is able to do that and then we could all see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have P2291? It is instead of the statement. And then page 3518, please. So six pages up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see the answer at the top of the first page. She said it was between 3.00 and 4.00. Then look at line 19: [In English] "You have testified that you had visited your mother at the hospital and you were on your way back." [Interpretation] So it is the Prosecutor's assertion that she had already testified that she was visiting her mother and she confirmed. Did you have this in mind when you entered it in your report?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what you can find in my report as I mentioned earlier on this morning for the sake of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours, I don't know about this, actually, because -- because on the page immediately prior to this, 3517, is the witness's actual evidence about why she went to the hospital. I just don't know if it's appropriate for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we leave it at that?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 3519, the next page. I'll read it out in English, from line 11: [In English] "At the moment that I was shot, I didn't even know that I was hit. I could just feel a blow, but I found out that I had been hit after I saw the bullets that were ricochetting from the concrete and I just continued to ride my bicycle and I managed to get home."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the witness here mention the ricochet?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as regards the previous part of her testimony when she said that bullets were falling around. A bullet fired from that distance hitting the concrete will ricochet. It is the nature of the round. There is always an angle. Irrespective of the fact whether she said so or not, it was definitely a ricochet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When talking about the church, can machine-guns have silencers?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Machine-guns do not have silencers. It is unnecessary, although it could be manufactured. However, if you have in mind the document we were shown, an anti-aircraft machine-gun was mentioned which is 12.7 millimetres in calibre, and the VRS did have it. You probably all saw the machine-gun. I can't tell off the cuff how long the barrel is but it's in total some 2 metres long and is carried by two people, and it has handles on the sides. I can't see how it could have been fitted in the church tower. The assumption is that there was the anti-aircraft machine-gun but I don't know where it could have been placed in the church tower because it's bigger than the size of the space in the tower itself. There is also no logic to use an observation point to mount an anti-aircraft machine-gun because the observation post is more important than the machine-gun which can be placed in a different location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there incidents or is there evidence that anybody in Dobrinja came to harm from that anti-aircraft machine-gun on the church tower?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When there was discussion about the incident involving Tarik Zunic, did Tarik -- or, rather, was Tarik Zunic there as instructed by security when you visited the site?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't have permission to go into houses or anything.
