In connection with incident number 2 at Sedrenik, I failed to say yesterday when Ms. Edgerton asked me if we were in that house, of course we were not because the witness is protected and it didn't cross our minds to disturb that person. We neither wanted to nor had permission to contact her.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the context of air-bombs and range error, can you tell us about the Grad missile? Can you express its range in percentages? What's the maximum range?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The maximum range is a little -- is just under 21 kilometres but you can say 21 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we express that as 100 per cent?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The distance indicated by Mr. Gaynor was 6.000 metres which is just above 30 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about a modified air-bomb? What's 100 per cent there?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about 10 kilometres, and the 6 kilometres in that case are about 60 per cent, maybe a bit over 60. It's closer to the maximum range. And that's where Mr. Gaynor made a mistake in the comparison because you must also take into consideration the relative relations because a dispersion depends on the maximum range. Let me give you an example. We have short range anti-tank missiles. Their range is 400 metres. If we were to apply the logic to compare it to the Grad missile at 6 kilometres, the dispersion would be such that it would be completely unusable.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, dealing with some technical issues, the interpreters will find it very difficult to follow. Could you speak very slowly? And could you repeat the last part, from Grad missiles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'll give you an example for shorter range missiles. Anti-tank missiles, the range of which is 400 metres, for example, are very precise at those distances. If we were to apply the same logic in comparing them to the Grad missiles, the result would be that they are very unprecise at these ranges because the dispersion depends on the maximum range. So we must consider the maximum range of any missiles and then we can compare the dispersion in percentages at the maximum range. If a missile has a short range, then the dispersion is small. I don't know if I was clear. The mistake Mr. Gaynor made when comparing the Grad missile at a range of 6.000 metres with a modified air-bomb at the same range is -- or, rather, consists in the following: He should have compared the Grad missile at 6.000 metres and the modified air-bomb at a range of about 2.000 metres, thereabouts. These values could be compared then because 6.000 metres is closer to the maximum range of a modified air-bomb than it is to the maximum range of the Grad missile. We saw from the firing tables that as the range rises, as the range increases, the range error probable diminishes. That's also a characteristic of the modified air-bomb. They are completely the same in these -- when it comes to the external ballistics characteristics, the same laws can be applied to both.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you express that in percentages of the range?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried absolute values. If we had a Grad missile --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is its error at 80 per cent of the maximum range and what's the value for the modified air-bomb?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The value should be roughly the same. If you had taken air-bomb at a range of about 2.000 metres, according to my rough calculation, the error would be more or less the same as that of the Grad missile at 6.000 metres. In relative terms it's about the same, only the distances are not the same, the absolute distances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us take a look at the diagram on page 73 in yesterday's testimony. It was not admitted, and I have a question concerning that diagram. If you would bear with me. It has to do with paragraph 164, between 134 and 146. Or maybe I can do that after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell me when the break is due?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: About ten past 12 or quarter past.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I will make an effort to finish by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 6 of yesterday's transcript, a heavy shell was mentioned. Can you tell me what kind of shell hit Markale? Was it two heavy shells or two light shells, and how do they differ?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was discussed on Friday. A heavy shell differs from a light shell, M72, first of all in its shape, the stabilisers. Markale was hit by a light shell, M62. I can tell by the stabilisers shown. Why did we mention this shell? Because UNPROFOR based its analysis on -- of the possibility of the radar being catching the shell on the M49 shell.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you repeat your last sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They used the firing tables for the M49 shell, and that is why we also used the M49 shell in our report, and we also gave a graphic firing tables for this shell, which show that the parameters stated in their comprehensive report were taken from the M49 shell firing table and more specifically for the basic charge. And that is a great mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could such a shell with the basic charge come from the Serbian positions and avoid the radar beam?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The maximum range of that shell is 1524 metres, if I remember correctly, and the separation line was about 2.000 metres away from the incident site. Another 500 metres were needed for such an M49 shell to reach that target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then the Serbian mortar must have been on the first line?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It must have been in the territory controlled by the BH Army. But the stabiliser also shows that it wasn't that shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see photograph 49 from Mr. Poparic's report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked about the centre of the radar beam. Please, can you indicate another centre in this photograph taking into account the lower limit of 548 metres. We must have a wider beam considering the constant value of 548.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the wrong image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are dealing with Subotic's report, co-authored by this witness. What's the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P3540.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It should be a D number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D3551, paragraph 109. Image 112.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us based on this diagram how UNPROFOR could have made that mistake and then I would like to display the image with the beam.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]

This roughly corresponds to this value. This is line 1. This is the trajectory of a shell fired from a distance of 950 metres. UNPROFOR says that it would certainly have been caught. If you look at the apex of that line, you will see that at these 548 metres -- but it's at 548 metres. That means that all trajectories above that would have been caught and any trajectory below that would not have. And they give another example. They say that a shell fired from 900 metres, that is a distance that is a bit shorter, would certainly have been caught by the radar beam. As you see, all trajectories with a shorter range of 950 have a greater ordinate, and they enter the radar beam. That is UNPROFOR's position. What is their greatest mistake? They used the same diagram and said if the ordinate is 548 here, but if we have a greater range and the maximum range is about 1500, I'll mark it here, what -- that's the trajectory of the shell with the maximum range. So if it's fired from a 1520 metres then it will go under the radar beam, which can be seen from this diagram. And finally, their conclusion was that all shells fired at a range from 1524 up to 3.000 metres would have gone under the radar beam. That is their greatest mistake. Why? Because firstly the trajectory I marked with the number 2, that is the trajectory at the maximum range, has a much smaller descent angle than 67 degrees. Maximum range trajectories have an initial angle of about 45 degrees - under ideal conditions, that is - and the angle of descent is a bit greater. So these trajectories must be ruled out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will read out the summary in the English language. [In English] Witness KW317 was an official of the Serbian Municipality of Zvornik. On 6th of April, 1992, the war broke out in Zvornik. He could hear the sound of mortars and tried to gather information as to what was happening. The Serbian members of the Zvornik police left Zvornik that day and arrived at the Alhos factory in Karakaj, reporting that they had been disarmed. On 8th of April, 1992, some Serbian leaders in Zvornik municipality went to Mali Zvornik to meet with the representatives of the Muslims. Before they could commence a private discussion about how to solve the problems, some armed people from Arkan's group arrived and took them to the municipal Assembly building in Mali Zvornik. Arkan called those Serb representatives traitors for negotiating with the Muslims, and his deputy, Peja, slapped and kicked some of them. Arkan then ordered that they be taken out of the building and be given ride from Mali Zvornik to Zvornik, and were told that politics was no longer for them. Arkan and his men launched an attack to liberate Zvornik. No one in the municipal government requested or authorised this attack. They had no means of contact with Radovan Karadzic at this time -- at that time, and the witness has no reason to believe that President Karadzic had any advanced knowledge of Arkan's attack or that he approved it. In Zvornik town, the witness observed that the only authority was the paramilitaries and they were the only persons you could see on the streets. The local authorities had no control over these paramilitaries. The paramilitaries were arresting and assaulting people and even established their own prisons. The lack of control by local -- the local authorities and the actions of the paramilitaries created fear among the citizens, mainly Muslims, but Serbs too. There were simply no officials who could protect the Muslims. During the next few months, some Muslim leaders from the village of Dulici, Kozluk and Sepak asked if the witness could protect them from the paramilitaries. The Kozluk Muslims got packed and ready to leave for Tuzla and witness wanted them to stay because it was never his objective to expel Muslims from Zvornik. The fights -- however, the fights intensified and got closer to Zvornik, and at that first -- tried to leave they had been visited by some representatives, Serb representatives, and their own objective was to dissuade them to leave and to persuade them to stay at their own homes. In this endeavour they had been helped by Serb bishop and two Muslim muftis, and they succeeded. The Muslims unpacked and stayed in Kozluk. Later on, because of those fights that got closer and closer to Kozluk and Zvornik, they decided to leave because there was no authorities who could guarantee them safety. The witness later informed President Karadzic and Krajisnik about what he had heard about the fate of the Muslims in Zvornik. President Karadzic was very disappointed and in what happened in Zvornik and expressed his disapproval. He had issued orders on several occasions that condemned any mistreatment or separation of civilians on any basis. It was never Republika Srpska or SDS party policy, either on a national or -- level or municipality level in Zvornik to expel Muslims. The civil war was the cause of the movement of the population. Those from Kozluk fortunately survived and returned from abroad to their own homes almost entirely. As part of an effort to establish some control in Zvornik on 17th of June, 1992, a war commission was appointed for Zvornik by President Radovan Karadzic in order to disband the interim government and restore the municipality assembly. On 13th of June, 1992, the witness attended a meeting at the municipal building -- Assembly building in Zvornik where President Karadzic and General Ratko Mladic also attended. During this meeting which was very brief because Karadzic and Mladic were in a rush, General Mladic expressed his strong disapproval of paramilitaries and threatened to arrest anyone who did not place themselves under the command of the army. President Karadzic stated that one of the most pressing tasks was to successfully establish civilian authorities reflecting the honesty and democratic qualities that characterise the Serbian people. The witness never understood President Karadzic to favour the expulsion of Muslims from the Serb territory. He finds it impossible to believe that President Karadzic would ever have favoured or condoned the execution of prisoners.

utterances.text: I did provide some objections, and, yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And those objections to a few of the items in the 2002 statement were reflected during the course of a taped interview which took place on that occasion and consisted of, as it turned out, some approximately 300 transcribed pages; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: I don't know how many pages there were, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But you recall that it was taped and it was a fairly long interview; right?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And you also testified in another proceeding in 2010; right?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, at paragraphs 9 and 10 of the statement you provided in this case, and that you just had -- is currently in front of you, you briefly described the establishment of the SDS and mentioned that it was not a classic party. I'm not certain what is meant by a classic party. So let's try to clarify a few basic things with some of the information that you provided before. First, it's correct, isn't it, as you stated in your 2002 interview, that very often the Main Board of the SDS would inform municipal boards about new decisions and conclusions?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if that involved confidential -- confidential material, confidential material from the Main Board was usually either collected by an official of the municipal board in Sarajevo or Pale or couriered in a closed envelope; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: I must make a slight correction. We did send documents by mail but we also carried them in person. If I was at Pale, for example, at the session of an assembly, and had some materials, I would carry them. If there was somebody else, then that other person would take it to the municipal board, if there were any materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And that was a reference to how confidential material or decisions and conclusions from the Main Board generally were conveyed down to the municipal level. On the other hand, going in the other direction, Brano Grujic, who was the president of the SDS party in Zvornik, would report the situation on the ground to the Main Board? And that's also information you provided at pages 9 and 10 of your 2002 interview.

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. You also advised that the SDS was a big party and had its own secretary who could be in daily communication with all of the people in the field, and that's right too, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: It did have a secretary but he couldn't be there all the time, but only when he was working, because otherwise one could understand it to mean that the man would sit there day and night and just wait for someone to contact him, and that's not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I don't think I understood and I don't think the Court understood that you were trying to convey that the man was there 24 hours a day every day of the year, but that basically he had the capacity to be in daily communication with the field as needed?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in Zvornik, too, there was a municipal secretary who basically worked every day and was in contact with local boards on essentially an everyday basis, and that's what you said in 2002; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Yes. It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, we just discussed briefly and in general decisions and conclusions transmitted to the municipal level from the top level of the SDS. And let me focus for a moment on one example that was discussed extensively in your previous interviews. It's correct, isn't it, that as the likelihood that Bosnia would pursue and obtain independence became greater in late 1991, that instructions known as commonly as Variant A and B were issued, that is the instructions for the organisation and activity of organs of Serbian people in emergency situation dated 19 December 1991?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: I'm familiar with Variants A and B. I remember them. But I don't know that those were instructions or orders to be implemented on the ground. It was information, like any other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, what I read to you was the title of the document. Let's call up P00005. It should be on the screen in front of you. You should see the first page. Okay. And as you explained in 2002, and affirmed again in 2003, that was received by the municipality, the SDS municipal board of Zvornik, and you saw a copy of it "probably within a few days of it being issued." That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Yes. I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And you also stated in that interview in 2002 and confirmed in 2003 that you were at a meeting of the Deputies Club where Radovan Karadzic, in the presence of Mr. Krajisnik, Mrs. Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic discussed instructions in this document, and that was at page 11 of your 2002 statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: I cannot recall that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, does this refresh your recollection? You also said that at that meeting that was the first time you heard about Variant A and B?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: No, I cannot confirm that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you want to see that statement or is my reciting it sufficient to test whether or not you can remember it at this time, remember saying those things to the OTP in 2002 and confirming it in 2003? So I can let you see the physical document or I can simply quote what you said.

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: I cannot remember now what I said and how, but I remember that I discussed that document. I remember that I discussed the document with the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's quickly call up, because we may have to refer to 60 -- I guess we have to go into private session for this, to call up 65 ter 22549.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, shall we move into private session briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sir, this will not be the first time that I confront you with things you said in 2002 and 2003 that are not compatible with the information you provided to this Chamber in that statement. You're asserting that you were under pressure and you were encouraged to say things that you didn't know were accurate. The 2003 interview in which you confirmed what you said in 2002 is on tape. You're welcome to look through that and find any reference to somebody telling you that you can just say whatever you want rather than asking to you look at the 2002 statement and confirm whether it's accurate. I will be asking you about that document. I will be pointing to assertions in the 2002 statement and the 2003 interview that bear on the statement you provided this Court today, and we'll march through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And with that in mind, I want to tender this excerpt that the witness saw in connection with the previous questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I don't have any objection to the excerpt, but I do have an objection to the speech that Mr. Tieger just made which is as improper if not more as things he claimed that Dr. Karadzic has done during his examination, and I trust that that won't be repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Could you give the page numbers, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Page 11 of both the English and B/C/S, Mr. President. And I think in the course of a cross-examination, when a witness makes an assertion that representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor encouraged him somehow or urged him to do something that is not reflected in the documents and the taped interview, I'm entitled to challenge him in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you are, but Mr. Robinson referred to the manner in which you should -- you do such challengings. Shall we receive the cover page and page 11? Yes, shall we assign the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6369 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Similarly, Witness, you explained in your 2002 interview, also at page 11, that the document "was immediately acted upon" by the members of the SDS municipal board; correct? That is the Variant A and B document.

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: At the outset I explained, we got that document and I saw it. We considered it. But it was not an order the way you phrased it right at the beginning or the way I understood you. It was not an order. It wasn't something that had to be implemented. Nobody had to submit a report about whether or not he implemented that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, you stated in 2002, did you not, and you confirmed in 2003, that the Variant A and B document was "immediately acted upon" by the members of the SDS municipal board, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Acted upon in what sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, for example, sir, this Court has received evidence -- that's P2590. Well, first of all the Variant A and B document calls for the establishment of Crisis Staffs, as I know you're aware, and we have received evidence, P2590, of the decision of the SDS Municipal Board to establish Crisis Staff and 24-hour watch on 22 December 1991, just a few days after this document. That's one. Similarly, P2591, another document this Court has received, is a decision regarding the formation of the Serbian Municipality of Zvornik on 27 December 1991 which explicitly states that it's based on the Variant A and B document. So those are two examples; right?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the Variant A and B document as we look through it and as I believe you will recall refers to two different types of municipalities, A and B, that is where Serbs are a majority and where Serbs are a minority, and also two levels, the first and second level of activation; right?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And with respect to the activation of the second level, you previously confirmed that you were present at a meeting, an extended session of the Deputies Club of the SDS on 14 February 1992 and, indeed, had an opportunity to read excerpts from the transcript of that session; right? And that's contained at page 72 of your 2003 interview.

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: I do not remember now what I said, but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you were shown in particular -- well, first of all, you recall the discussion I take it about the February 14th meeting and confirming that you were present at that meeting; right?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: I don't know which meeting you mean, the 14th of February, the meeting of which body?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that's the meeting at which, as the transcript of that meeting reveals, Dr. Karadzic made four separate references to the second level or stage number 2 including ending a portion of his speech by saying, That's why we called you here. Please, that is why we called you today to intensify, to introduce the second level and to intensify the functioning of the government at any cost and on every single millimetre of our territory. That's the meeting. Okay. You recall that now?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: I cannot recall, but if it was an assembly meeting -- I mean you have to be more precise. Was it an assembly meeting or a Main Board meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: An extended session of the Deputies Club which means it included Main Board representatives and municipal representatives.

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: I do not remember the meeting itself, but we should take a look at the dates. If we just look at things as you're suggesting, without a context, it's very dangerous or risky to interpret them, and what event is it about? If there was talk about the Cutileiro plan to resolve the situation in Bosnia and it's taken out of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not taking anything out of context. I am focusing on what you -- the information that that you previously provided back at a time when these events as you indicated were much fresher in your memory. So you were shown, and that's reflected at page 72 of your interview in 2003, the excerpts from that assembly after indicating that you were present there and were asked if this is the second level of activation that is -- that he's referring to, that is, is that the second level of Variant A and B and you said, "I think that's precisely what he's referring to." Similarly, sir, you explained that a, quote, directive that is concerning the activation of the second level was received prior to March 15, 1992 "I think it was a fax maybe a letter." And that's reflected at page 79 of your 2003 interview. You also explained at page 87 of that interview that with respect to that directive, there weren't many, quote: "There weren't many instructions. It was simply said in there that the conditions in Bosnia-Herzegovina were such that we should begin implementation of the second level of the second level from the instructions to municipalities A and B." And that's page 87 of your 2003 interview. And as I will tell you in a minute you also referred to what the SDS authorities in Zvornik did to implement that directive. That's all correct, isn't it, sir? That's what you told the OTP in 2003 on tape?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: That may be correct, but I've repeated several times my remark about the context. I don't know what event was discussed at that meeting, and that's why it's very difficult to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: (redacted) Witness, I went through the fairly painstakingly telling you about the February 14th meeting, the nature of that meeting, reminding you that at that meeting Mr. Karadzic gave a speech during which he made four separate references to level 2 or stage number 2, that you confirmed in 2003 that that was a reference to the second level of the Variant A and B document, that you then went on to say there was a directive subsequently received but before March 15th, that you explained what that said. It didn't provide many instructions, it just said that we should begin implementation of the second level, and then as I indicated you went on to indicate what Zvornik -- the Zvornik SDS authorities did to implement it. That should be sufficient context, sir, for you to understand the questions I'm asking you; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And do you -- it's also correct, sir, that in 2003, you had an opportunity to review a bundle of documents, they were called, reflecting decisions made at the 15 March 1992 session of the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Zvornik, and you confirmed at page 29, part 2, of the 2003 interview, that these decisions were made in accordance with the activation of the second level of the Variant A and B instructions?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you referred to the Cutileiro Plan a few moments ago and you also referred to that in paragraph 31 of your statement. I take it then that you will recall that on March 18, 1992, the same date of the agreement in principle between the Cutileiro participants, that there was an extensive discussion in the Bosnian Serb Assembly which focused almost exclusively on the Cutileiro Plan during which a number of people expressed concern about Muslim intentions or SDA intentions regarding the plan, and suggested, that is even more people suggested, that pragmatic steps on the ground in addition to the negotiations should be taken. You remember that meeting, sir, and that discussion? This Court has actually received evidence of -- of that meeting. They have the transcript of that session of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you further recall that as the imminence of the independence of Bosnia became even more pronounced, that is as events moved even closer to the beginning of April, there were further discussions about what the Bosnian Serb authorities should do and when? So, for example, at the 12th assembly session held on March 24th, 1992, Dr. Karadzic stated, This will be very soon, we can form whatever we want. And as an example he said: "The Zvornik municipality takes control over everything that constitutes the Serbian Municipality of Zvornik, then at a given moment in the next three or four days there will be a single method used and you will be able to apply it in the municipalities you represent including both things that must be done as well as how to do them, how to separate the police force, take the resources that belong to the Serbian people, and take command." That's P961, and he also spoke about the establishment of "actual and sovereign authority" on the ground "as soon as possible." Stating, I ask you now that following some instructions for National Defence information systems, et cetera, that will be given here, the real and sovereign authority of the Serbian Assembly and Serbian people be established on the ground as soon as possible and he spoke about then what happens as -- when we have our own separate MUP, and so on. That's -- you said in 2003, when shown that excerpt "what is meant here is to implement the instructions in item B." That's at page 95 through 96 of your 2003 interview; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: That's right, but you have not been making any comments whatsoever in terms of what happened before these meetings. You are not saying anything about what agreement was being sought on within Bosnia. You are just saying what Karadzic says, what Krajisnik says. That's what I discussed at the OTP, too, and that's what I object to. This is not the consequence of the will of Karadzic or at the Main Board or people at the SDS. These established bodies in the assembly, that was the result of what the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina wanted to do. Had you investigated their side you would have found a multitude of documents speaking about these same things too, but you did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is all -- this was all forced on you and Mr. Karadzic and the SDS; right? That's your position?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: It was forced.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just so you know, Witness, you're not the first witness to appear here and the Court has received a great deal of information about what was happening at that particular time, what happened in the months previous, what happened in the period following, including but certainly not limited to everyone of the Bosnian Serb Assembly sessions during which this issue was described, and including the testimony of many witnesses about the events that preceded and followed the outbreak of the conflict. So that is -- I won't be seeking all that information from you, and you had the opportunity to present much of it in your statement. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The witness was able to answer your previous question but in the future, could you break down into some shorter questions so that we can follow better?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Also, Mr. President, this last comment is really inappropriate, and Mr. Tieger shouldn't be expecting to get any additional time if he's going to spend his time arguing with the witness without asking any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's get on with cross-examination. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. President, it's a very unfair intervention when a witness wants to know what's essentially the context of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, at paragraphs 35 through 48 of your statement, you discuss in -- okay, sir, you have your hand up in a manner that indicates I think you want to ask a question. Normally witnesses don't ask questions, but if it's something you need to add to what you said --

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: But I have to -- I feel the need to add something. In this situation in which you're putting such questions, taken out of -- I mean, to this day I claim that this is taken out of context. I cannot recall all of those details, and I cannot interpret Karadzic's speeches to you. You have to interpret them with him. But I don't see what preceded that and what a particular meeting was devoted to. If you just say that we met and to discuss Variants A and B, that's what it seems like, but no way, you're not saying what preceded this, what happened before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Again, at paragraphs 35 through 48 of your statement, you discuss events of 6 April through 9 April, during which the Crisis Staff declared a state of war, Arkan's men, led by Peja arrived, the meeting in Mali Zvornik took place, and you also refer to Marko Pavlovic without -- for the first time without explaining who he was and explain something about the arrival of Arkan. Now I want to ask you some questions about both Pavlovic and Arkan. First of all, as we just indicated, your statement notes that he arrived at least on this occasion just as the conflict was beginning, in that period of April. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Arkan?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Oh, Pavlovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And shortly thereafter he became commander of the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Municipality of Zvornik; right?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, he had first been -- that is, Pavlovic had first been introduced to SDS people in Zvornik by Dragan Spasojevic and introduced as a businessman, and that happened in December of 1991, when the Serbian municipality was formed; right?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. But it was "very clear" to you, even as early as April 1992, when Pavlovic showed up again, that he was no businessman; right? That he was there --

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Well, that is basically correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, this Trial Chamber has received evidence that Pavlovic was a member of the Serbian State Security Service or DB, that can be found at P2848. And, Witness, you also concluded that he was a member of a security organ?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Not Serbia but the former state, the federal organs of the former state of Yugoslavia. That's what I think to this day, that this was related to the JNA and the federal organs, not Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You understood him to be a security official and not -- that his introduction as a businessman was a kind of cover for that?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. And although you believe that it was Mr. Spasojevic who brought Pavlovic to Zvornik, you also noted that he was "on good terms with Brano Grujic as well"; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: For the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in any event, Pavlovic and Mr. Grujic co-operated right away from the beginning?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: They were together most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, that's what you said in 2003 as well. They worked together and you further advised that they were the two main or most powerful figures in the municipality, as you said, it was Grujic and Pavlovic who had "the main say" in the municipality. That's the position --

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And in addition to his position as president of the SDS, which you noted in paragraph 8 of your statement, and his position as commander or president of the Crisis Staff, Mr. Grujic became the head of the interim or provisional or temporary government; right?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to that temporary or provisional government or war government, it was actually Pavlovic who suggested a temporary war government, and he did so at a meeting on April 10th; right?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And he explained that "based on our experience from Western Slavonia" that was the best way to proceed, that in -- that what had happened there is that all legally elected authorities and bodies were frozen and annulled. It is much better to set up a provisional wartime government, much more efficient; right?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And after Pavlovic explained that this is how it had been done successfully before, that proposal was adopted; right?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 45 of your statement, you say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. President. Maybe we should go into private session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as long as you mention Mr. Radic, let me just note that his job was to disburse or pay out funds due by the temporary government; right?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say exactly now what his job was. I think he was the secretary of that government, and perhaps finance went through him. That's possible. That's possible that finance went through him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In any event, he was often seen with members of various paramilitary groups "in very good spirits as you put it in 2003," and you concluded that Radic had a special relationship with them [Realtime transcript read in error "him"]; right?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Well, I cannot claim that he had a special relationship but that he was seen with them. That's true. But a special relationship? I don't think so. I mean, I don't have any proof of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tieger said [In English] "Radic had a special relationship with him." [Interpretation] And the interpretation the witness received was "with them."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was intending to say with them. That's what the transcript says. So -- and I'll quote it again. You were asked at page 234 whether Radic had a special relationship with any of the paramilitary groups. You explained what you heard him talking about, their treatment of him and their greed: "From which I concluded that he did have a special relationship with them and he was often seen with those men and he seemed to be in very good spirits."

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Well, you see now you put it right. I said what I heard. I did not claim that they had any special kind of relationship. I wasn't saying that I concluded something. Well, you can conclude something on the basis of something you heard, couldn't you? But I personally did see them with him. But I cannot claim on the basis of that that he had a special relationship with them because I don't know what kind of relations he had with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also indicated that people like Mr. Grujic, Mr. Radic, were less in favour of negotiations than you and more supportive of establishing a situation where the Serbian municipality could assume authority on the ground; correct? That's found at page 120 of the 2003 interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, I know it -- maybe we should -- please be cautious, sir.

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Let's just proceed. I was simply trying to contrast what you stated earlier in 2003 about the views of people like Grujic and Radic, who were not in favour of negotiations, but -- or at least less supportive of negotiations and more supportive of establishing a situation where Serbian municipality could assume authority on the ground. That's a correct contrast between the two views, right, without talking about the details of your personal involvement at this point?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: But -- but I basically meant the Crisis Staff meeting when it was decided to go to negotiate, at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's be clear in the -- about one thing and that is about the reality of dividing Zvornik. And you have previously stated, and made very clear, that it was not possible to divide the municipality because there were Muslim and Serb villages mixed throughout the territory; right? You couldn't divide Zvornik "by the ethnic principle." An ethnic map of Zvornik is "not possible to make." Those are all things you said before and those are all accurate; right?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but -- well, that is correct, but look, we have to get this clear. It wasn't possible to make an ethnic division down a straight line like this because this is a zig-zag line where it's not possible exactly to draw this boundary everywhere. That's what was meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 65 ter 002420, please. It's 002420 -- I'm sorry, O, not zero, that's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's a map depicting the ethnic distribution in Zvornik based on the 1991 census. And, sir, that's really a reflection of the nature of the Zvornik municipality. Even setting aside questions of distribution of large companies like Glinica and Birac, that's a reflection of the impossibility of dividing Zvornik in any kind of meaningful way, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6370, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, at paragraphs 38 through 41 of your statement, you indicate that Pavlovic and Arkan's men and Arkan came at basically the same time, in that limited time at the beginning of April; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: No, no, no. They came -- Arkan came, I first saw him then when that thing happened in Mali Zvornik, and there is no doubt about that, that's exactly the way it was. As for Pavlovic, Pavlovic came before he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So Pavlovic came a couple of times. First he came with Spasojevic when the Serbian municipality was declared in December of 1991, then he came back at the beginning of April, right, shortly before this Mali Zvornik meeting?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Well, maybe at the very beginning, when we went to Alhos, that's when he showed up. That's how I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And by the way, at that Mali Zvornik meeting, you were able to recognise Arkan from pictures you'd seen on television and in newspapers because he was dressed in the same way. He had -- you had seen him dressed in Croatia and also in Bijeljina; right? And you had stated that in 2002?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you were also able to conclude with respect to Pavlovic and Arkan, based on your -- and Arkan's men, including Peja, based on your observations of their interactions and what they said and how they worked together, that they were part of the same team; right?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Well, it may be concluded that they were an interest group but the same team? I cannot say. But the same interest group at the time, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, back in 2002, basically you stated that a number of times, so in 2002, at page 20, you stated, "So my conclusion was that he was part of the same team that Arkan belonged to." You also stated in 2003, Marko Pavlovic came "in advance of paramilitary units and after him they arrived in numbers, and his later role told me that he was on the same team." And later in making another -- that's at page 162. And a later in making another point, you stated that, "Since he worked on the same team as Arkan," and then went on to make your point. So in 2002 and 2003, you repeatedly stated that Pavlovic and Arkan were on the same team; correct? At least those were your conclusions based on what you saw?

utterances.speaker: KW317
utterances.text: Yes, I probably said that it was the same team but if you mean that team is a sort of staff or a group that has an exactly set task, perhaps it would be better to say the same interest group because I do not have any proof that they were sitting in some staff and that he were -- that they were appointed to be such and such and such a team. I mean it would be illogical to assert anything like that because I don't have that kind of proof, but that they were the same interest group, they were. And that would be my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Good time to break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that's it for today. Mr. Witness, we will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. I'd like to advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. The hearing is adjourned.
